lines.t: Okay everyone, eyes up here, let's get started.
Can we sit wherever?

You're already sitting, so yes, that works. Today we're going to learn about the Stamp Act and this idea of "no taxation without representation." By the end of class, you will be able to explain why the colonists were so upset about this tax, and who actually had to pay it. This connects to stuff we've talked about before with Parliament and the colonies, so let's dig in.
Is this going to be on the test?

It might show up, so pay attention. Let's start with some background. After the French and Indian War, Britain was in a ton of debt. Parliament figured the colonies should help pay for it since British soldiers had been defending them. So in 1765, Parliament passed a new law called the Stamp Act.
What was the Stamp Act?
A tax on paper stuff!
Good job, yes, a tax on printed materials like newspapers, legal documents, even playing cards.
My dad has old playing cards.
Interesting, but let's stay focused. So every time someone bought one of these paper items, they had to buy a stamp to put on it, proving they paid the tax.
Who had to pay it?
The colonists!
Right, nice work. All the colonists had to pay this tax, not just certain people.
How many colonies were there at this time?
Thirteen!
Exactly, thirteen colonies, good job.
And when did Parliament pass the Stamp Act?
Right, 1765, you guys are on fire today.
I think it was also because—
It made everyone really mad because they didn't get a vote!
Good job, that's exactly right, they didn't get a say in this.
What does representation mean?
Like having a voice in government.
Nice work, yes, representation means having someone speak for you, vote for you, in the government that's making the laws.
So what did the colonists start saying about this?
No taxation without representation!

Exactly, that's the big phrase. "No taxation without representation" became their rallying cry. The colonists believed that if Parliament was going to tax them, they should at least have representatives in Parliament voting on their behalf. But they didn't have any representatives there at all.
That's so unfair.
It does seem unfair, doesn't it? Let's keep going. The colonists were furious, and they didn't just complain quietly. They organized protests, boycotts, and even threatened the stamp collectors.
Who remembers what a boycott is?
Not buying stuff!
Good job, a boycott means refusing to buy or use certain goods to make a political point.
Define the word "repeal."
To cancel a law?

Close, but let's be more exact — it means to officially cancel or get rid of a law. And that's actually what happened here, Parliament repealed the Stamp Act in 1766 because the protests were working.
So it worked?
It did work, good question, but it didn't fix everything, because Parliament still believed they had the right to tax the colonies whenever they wanted.
Eyes up here please, I'm hearing side conversations.
Sorry!
It's okay, let's refocus. I need everyone looking at me for this next part, because it's important.
Why do you think the colonists were so angry about a tax on paper?
Because they had no choice!
I think it was more about—
And it was on everything, like even newspapers!
Good job, yes, it touched basically everything they read and wrote, which made it feel really invasive.
What else made them angry, besides not having representation?
They felt like Britain didn't trust them.
Nice thinking, that's a great point actually.
Let's look at a short primary source now. I want you to read this quietly to yourselves. It's a quote from a colonial pamphlet about the Stamp Act. Take ninety seconds to read it carefully.
Okay, let's bring it back together.
What was the main complaint in that pamphlet?
They said Parliament had no right to tax them.
Exactly, good job, that's the core argument.
What does the phrase "virtual representation" mean?
That Britain said they already represented the colonies?
Right, nice work, Britain argued that Parliament represented all British subjects everywhere, even without actual elected colonial representatives. The colonists didn't buy that argument at all.
That's a dumb argument.
It's definitely a weak one, I'd agree. Let's keep moving.
Who were the Sons of Liberty?
The group that protested!
Good job, yes, they were a group of colonists who organized protests and sometimes used intimidation against stamp collectors.
Quiet please, I need everyone to settle down for a second.
Sorry, Ms. Carter.
It's fine, let's keep our voices down though. So the Sons of Liberty were really influential in making the Stamp Act impossible to enforce.
What happened to a lot of the stamp collectors?
They quit because people threatened them!
Right, exactly, many resigned out of fear, good job.
Why do you think Parliament eventually backed down and repealed the law?
Because the protests were hurting business?
That's a great point, yes, British merchants were losing money because of the boycotts, so they pressured Parliament to repeal it.
I was going to say something like that.
Go ahead, Jordan, finish your thought.
I just think it's cool that regular people had that much power.
I like how you said that, that's a really good point, thank you Jordan.

Let's talk about what came next. Even though the Stamp Act was repealed, Parliament passed the Declaratory Act, which said they still had full power to make laws for the colonies. So the conflict wasn't over, it just kind of paused.
What was passed right after the Stamp Act was repealed?
The Declaratory Act!
Good job, nice recall.
Stop talking, guys, I need quiet for this next part.
It wasn't me!
I believe you, let's just focus up please.
So, in other words, Britain was saying, "fine, we'll remove this specific tax, but we still control you." That's a key term you'll want to remember — the Declaratory Act.
What does the word "repeal" mean again, quick recall?
To cancel it!
Good job, exactly.
Thumbs up if that makes sense so far?
Okay, I see some thumbs, not everybody, but let's keep moving, we'll come back to it.
Define "taxation" for me.
Making people pay money to the government.
Nice work, that's right.
Where did most of the protests against the Stamp Act happen?
In the colonies, like Boston!
Good job, Boston especially was a hotspot for protest.
Who was the king of England at this time?
King George the Third!
Right, nice work, King George the Third.
What was one way colonists protested besides boycotting?
Burning stuff, like effigies!
Good job, yes, they sometimes burned effigies of tax collectors or officials.
That's kind of intense.
It was, people felt really strongly.

So let's connect this to something bigger. Think about a time when you felt like a decision was made about you without you having any say. Maybe a rule at school, or something at home. That's kind of how the colonists felt, but on a much bigger scale, with their money and their rights.
Like when they changed our lunch schedule without asking us!
Exactly, that's a perfect example, nice thinking.
So what's the big lesson the colonists learned from the Stamp Act crisis?
That protesting works!
Good job, that they could push back and actually make change happen.
And remember, this is just the start. The tension between the colonies and Britain is going to keep building after this, and we'll talk about other taxes they tried next time.
What was today's big vocabulary term again, the main one?
Taxation without representation!
Good job, exactly, that's the one I want you to remember.
Okay, before you leave, I want you to write down one sentence on your exit ticket explaining why the colonists were upset about the Stamp Act.
Alright, let's collect those on your way out.
Do we turn it in at the door?
Yes, hand it in on your way out please.
This was actually kind of interesting.
I'm glad to hear that, good job today everyone, see you tomorrow.
Okay, everyone, eyes up here for a second before we dive in.

So last week I noticed something — you all know this material really, really well. But I also noticed the same four or five hands going up every single time. I love that you all know this stuff, but I want to hear from more voices, so here's how questions work now.

Here's the new rule. I'm going to ask a question, you're going to get quiet time to write your own answer, then a quick turn and talk, and then I'm going to call on people by name — including people who don't usually raise their hands. And if you call out before I call your name, you lose your turn, and I'll come back to you later. Everybody clear on that?
So we can't just yell it out anymore?
Nope. Everyone gets think time first. It's not a race.
Our goal for today is to figure out whether the Boston Tea Party was protest or vandalism, and to back up our opinion with real evidence from what we've learned about colonial boycotts.
Let's start simple. What is a boycott?
Take thirty seconds and write down your answer.
Turn and talk with your neighbor for ten seconds.
Marcus, can you read me what you wrote?
I wrote that a boycott is when people refuse to buy something to make a point or hurt a company's money.
Nice work. Boycott means that people are using their money, or their refusal to spend it, as a form of protest. I like that you connected it to hurting profits, Marcus.
Next question. What was being taxed under the Townshend Acts?
Take thirty seconds and write down your answer.
Turn and talk with your neighbor for ten seconds.
Glass, paint, paper, and tea!
Hold that thought — I want to hear from Maya first.
I wrote glass, paint, paper, and tea, and the colonists were mad because they didn't vote for those taxes.
Great job, Maya. That's exactly right, and I like how you added the reasoning part too — no taxation without representation.
Why do you think the colonists specifically targeted tea for their protest, out of all those goods?
Take thirty seconds and write down your answer.
Turn and talk with your neighbor for ten seconds.
Jayden, what did you write?
I think they picked tea because almost everybody drank it, so if they dumped tea it would get the most attention and hurt the company the most.
What makes you say that, the attention part?
Because if it was something nobody cared about, nobody would've talked about it afterward.
Love that reasoning. You're thinking about this like a strategist, not just a historian.
Let's go back — Danny, you had your hand up earlier. What were you going to say about the Townshend Acts?
Oh — just that tea was the one tax they kept after they got rid of the others.
Good catch, that's true, they repealed most of them but kept the tea tax standing as a symbol.
Who is the group that organized and carried out the Boston Tea Party?
Take thirty seconds and write down your answer.
Turn and talk with your neighbor for ten seconds.
Priya, go ahead.
I wrote the Sons of Liberty, they were the group led by Samuel Adams that organized protests against British taxes.
Excellent, Priya. The word Sons of Liberty is our key term for today, so hold onto that.
Here's a bigger one. How would a loyalist, someone still loyal to the king, see the Boston Tea Party?
Take thirty seconds and write down your answer.
Turn and talk with your neighbor for ten seconds.
Omar, what did you write?
A loyalist would probably see it as stealing and destroying private property, not protest, because it wasn't their tea to dump.
What evidence from the reading backs that up?
The reading said the tea belonged to the East India Company, not the king, so loyalists would say innocent business owners got hurt.
Great point, Omar. That's exactly the kind of evidence-based thinking I want.
What would happen if the colonists had just paid the tea tax instead of dumping it?
Take thirty seconds and write down your answer.
Turn and talk with your neighbor for ten seconds.
Let's hear from someone we haven't heard from yet. Lily?
I think if they paid it, Britain would think they could keep taxing them without asking, so the protests probably would've gotten worse later anyway.
Nice thinking, Lily. So you're saying giving in might've made things worse down the line, not better?
Yeah, because then Britain learns they can just push and push.
Define the word vandalism for me — what does that actually mean?
Take thirty seconds and write down your answer.
Turn and talk with your neighbor for ten seconds.
Carlos, read yours.
Vandalism is defined as destroying or damaging someone's property on purpose without permission.
Good job. So keep that definition in your head as we keep comparing it to what happened in the harbor.
Have you ever seen a protest on the news, maybe people blocking a road or something like that?
Yeah, my mom said people blocked a highway once about something at her job.
Think about a time like that — was it legal? Probably not. Does that automatically make it wrong?
I don't think so, because sometimes people feel like it's the only way to get noticed.
That connects really well to tonight's — I mean today's — big question.
Why do you think some historians call the Tea Party the first act of the American Revolution?
Take thirty seconds and write down your answer.
Turn and talk with your neighbor for ten seconds.
Keisha, what did you write?
I wrote that it was the first time colonists took direct action instead of just writing letters or boycotting, so it changed how serious things got.
What makes you say it changed how serious things got?
Because after that, Britain punished them hard with the Intolerable Acts, so it escalated everything.
I like how you used the word escalated there — that's a great way to describe it.
Okay, settle down for a second, I know we're getting excited — let's keep our voices at discussion level so everyone can hear each other.
Next question. How could the Boston Tea Party be seen as both protest and vandalism at the same time?
Take thirty seconds and write down your answer.
Turn and talk with your neighbor for ten seconds.
Maya, you again?
I think it's both because they were protesting unfair taxes, but they still destroyed property that wasn't theirs, so both things are true at once.
I really like how you used the word boycott earlier to explain why the merchants lost money, Maya, and now you're holding two ideas at once — that's exactly the kind of complexity we want.
Defend your answer — was the East India Company an innocent victim, or part of the problem?
Take thirty seconds and write down your answer.
Turn and talk with your neighbor for ten seconds.
Danny, now it's your turn — go ahead.
I wrote that the company wasn't totally innocent because they worked with the British government to get special deals that hurt colonial merchants.
Nice work, Danny, and thanks for waiting your turn earlier too. What evidence did you use for that?
The reading said the Tea Act let them sell tea cheaper than other merchants, so colonial sellers were getting squeezed out.
Great connection. That squeeze is part of why merchants joined the protest, not just regular colonists.
Last one before we wrap up. Compare the Boston Tea Party to a protest you've learned about or seen today — what's similar, and what's different?
Take thirty seconds and write down your answer.
Turn and talk with your neighbor for ten seconds.
Jayden, close us out.
It's similar because people are angry about unfair treatment and want to be heard, but it's different because today most protests don't destroy property on purpose.
Awesome, Jayden. That's a thoughtful way to end our discussion today.
Before you leave, write one reason the Tea Party was protest and one reason it wasn't, and hand it to me on your way out.
Can it be short?
Yep, just a sentence for each is perfect.
Great job today, everyone — I heard so many more voices than usual, and that's exactly what I was hoping for.
Okay, eyes up here, let's get started. Our goal for today is to practice writing strong analysis using evidence, specifically around the scene with Candy's dog in chapter three.
Before we dive in, what happens when Carlson wants to take Candy's dog outside?
Carlson says the dog is old and smells bad and he wants to just shoot it because it's not useful anymore.
Good job, that's exactly the setup. Now, what is Candy's reaction when Carlson first brings it up?
Candy doesn't want him to do it, he keeps making excuses like maybe it'll get better.
Nice work. So here's our claim for today, I'm putting it up on the board. Steinbeck shows that in this world, anything that stops being useful is thrown away.

We're going to use a sentence frame to build our analysis. It goes, "this is shown when blank, because blank." The "when" is your evidence, the "because" is your thinking — that's the part that actually matters most.
So why do you think Steinbeck chose a dog, specifically, to show this idea instead of something else?
Maybe because a dog is supposed to be loyal and loved, so it's sadder when even that gets thrown away for being old.
Okay, but why does that matter for the bigger picture of the novel?
Because it makes you think, if even a loyal dog isn't safe, then people who aren't useful anymore probably aren't safe either.
Love that connection. Hold that thought, you're going to need it in a minute. Talk to your partner and find your "shown when" — remember, I want the because too.
Okay, let's hear some of what you found. Who wants to share first?
This shows that the dog is thrown away when Carlson says it's got no teeth and it stinks and it ain't no good to Candy no more.
Good start. Okay, but why does that matter? What's the "because"?
Because it shows Carlson only cares about what something is worth, not about feelings or loyalty or how long it's been around.
Excellent, that's the because. How does that connect to George and Lennie?
Because Lennie isn't useful either, in a way, since he messes things up, so maybe the same thing could happen to him.
That is such a sharp read ahead. I like how you connected it already, hold onto that for later chapters.
Who else found a "shown when"?
This shows that Candy feels powerless when he just lays down and doesn't look at the dog while Carlson takes it outside.
What evidence from the text makes you say he's powerless, not just sad?
He doesn't argue after a certain point, he just stops talking, and that silence kind of shows he's given up fighting it.
Great point. What would happen if Candy had said no, and really meant it?
Maybe Carlson would've backed off, since nobody else really wanted to do it either, they were kind of waiting for permission.
How does that connect to the claim on the board?
Because it shows the men go along with throwing things away even when they don't totally want to, like it's just expected.
Really strong thinking. That idea of things being "expected" is going to come back later in the book.
Let's push a little further. How might this scene predict what happens later with other characters?
It kind of foreshadows something bad, since the dog getting shot feels like a warning for someone else getting treated the same way.
Great word, "foreshadows." Let's define that. Foreshadowing is defined as when an author gives hints earlier in a story about something that's going to happen later.
So, knowing that definition, why do you think Steinbeck included Carlson's reaction right after the dog is shot?
Because Carlson doesn't really react much, and that shows how normal it is on the ranch to just get rid of things that slow you down.
Nice thinking. How does the men's reaction, or lack of one, reveal what the ranch actually values?
It shows the ranch values usefulness over loyalty, since nobody really defends the dog once Carlson makes his case.
Okay, but why does that matter for Candy specifically, later in the chapter?
Because Candy gets scared it'll happen to him too, once he's too old to work, so he asks about the land with George and Lennie.
That's it exactly. You just connected the dog scene straight to Candy's choice to join the dream. That's the because that actually does work.
Let's hear one more "shown when" before we move on.
This shows that the dog's death is treated like a chore when Carlson says it so plain, like it ain't a big deal to him at all.
Okay, but why does that matter? What's underneath that calmness?
Because it shows how numb people get to cruelty when it happens over and over, like it's just normal life on the ranch.
Wow. "Numb to cruelty" — write that phrase down, that's strong vocabulary for your paragraph.
Let's check in. Fist to five, how ready are you to write this "shown when, because" on your own?
I'd say like a four, I think I got the evidence part, I'm just not sure my because is deep enough yet.
That's honest, and totally fine, that's what we're building today.
I'm at a five, I think I finally get what "because" is supposed to do now.
Love hearing that. What changed for you?
Before I was just repeating the quote, but now I get that because has to say why it matters, not just what happened.
That's the whole lesson right there, you just said it better than I could have.
I'm at a three, I keep writing the "when" part really long and forgetting the "because" completely.
That's super common, and a great thing to notice about your own writing.
Alright, let's try one more, a harder one. Why do you think Steinbeck waited until this chapter to show us this, instead of earlier in the book?
Maybe because by now we already like Candy, so it hits harder, and we understand the ranch better too.
Great point, timing changes how we feel about it. How would the scene feel different if it happened in chapter one?
It probably wouldn't feel as sad, since we wouldn't know Candy yet, we'd just see it as some guy losing his dog.
Exactly, Steinbeck is building our sympathy on purpose. That's intentional craft, not an accident.
Last one, and this is a tough one. Defend your claim — what's the strongest piece of evidence in the whole chapter for "anything that stops being useful is thrown away"?
I think it's when Carlson says the dog ain't no good to himself, because that's the exact logic that gets used against Candy later.
That's a strong, well-defended claim. You used the text and connected it forward. That's exactly the kind of because I want in your writing.
Okay, before you leave, write your own "shown when, because" sentence using a different piece of evidence than the one you shared out loud today.
Can it be about Lennie instead of Candy?
Absolutely, as long as you've got a real "when" and a real "because" behind it.
Does the because have to connect to George and Lennie, or can it just explain the quote?
It can do either, but the strongest ones usually do both — that's the difference between good and great today.
Great job today, everyone. I really liked how many of you pushed past the first answer and found the deeper "because." That's exactly the skill we're building toward for your essay.
Okay, good afternoon, everyone. I know it's eighth period, it's been a long day, but let's get started.

Today we are going to look at the causes of the Industrial Revolution. By the end of class, you will be able to name at least three causes of industrialization and explain why Britain was the first country to industrialize.
Let's start with a quick review. Last week we talked about farming in Europe before the eighteenth century.
What was farming like in Europe before the eighteenth century?
No one? That's okay. Farming back then was mostly small plots, worked by hand, with pretty low crop yields. Families grew just enough to survive, and there wasn't a lot of extra food left over.
So new tools and farming techniques started to change that. What are some things you think changed once crop yields increased?
More food for everyone?
Good, more food for everyone. That's exactly right.

When crop yields go up, population tends to grow too, because fewer people are dying from starvation or disease. This is called the Agricultural Revolution, and it happened right before the Industrial Revolution in Britain.
Why do you think a growing population matters for industrialization?
More workers for factories.
Nice thinking, Derek. More workers for factories, exactly.
With more people than farms could employ, a lot of families moved to cities looking for work. That created a huge pool of labor ready to work in the new factories that were starting to open up.
What was the enclosure movement?
I'll explain. The enclosure movement was when wealthy landowners in Britain fenced off common lands that used to be shared by everyone in a village.
That pushed a lot of small farmers off the land they used to work.
So those farmers had no choice but to move to cities and look for factory work. That connects right back to the idea of population and labor we just talked about.
Let's talk about vocabulary for a second. The word surplus is a key term for today. The definition of surplus is an amount of something left over after what's needed has already been used.
Can anyone use surplus in a sentence about farming?
Farmers had surplus crops to sell?
Great job, Priya. Exactly, farmers had a surplus of crops, so they could sell the extra instead of just feeding their own families.
Now let's talk about capital. Capital, in this case, means money or wealth that can be invested into something, like building a factory.
What are some places Britain got that capital from?
Trading and colonies?
Good, trading and colonies. That's a big part of it.
Britain had a huge colonial empire, so they had access to raw materials, things like cotton from India and sugar from the Caribbean.
They also made a lot of money from trade, including, unfortunately, the slave trade. All of that profit became capital wealthy merchants could invest into new businesses and new machines.
Britain also had something going for it geographically. Name the two natural resources Britain had a lot of, close together.
Coal and iron.
Exactly, coal and iron. Nice work.
Coal was used to power steam engines, and iron was used to build machines and later railroads. Britain had both of these close together, which made it cheap and easy to mine and move them around.
Why do you think Britain industrialized first, before other countries in Europe?
Because they had resources and money?
That's a great point, Priya. Resources, capital, labor, Britain really had all the pieces in place at the same time.
Other countries, like France and Germany, had some of these factors too, but not all of them together in quite the same way, at least not yet.
Let's talk about technology now. New inventions were a huge part of what made the Industrial Revolution possible.
Raise your hand if you've heard of the spinning jenny.
Just a few of you, okay.
The spinning jenny was a machine invented in 1764 by James Hargreaves. It let one worker spin multiple threads of cotton at once instead of just one thread by hand.
That made cloth production so much faster, and it's one of the inventions that really kicked off the textile industry in Britain.
You might have seen pictures of old factories with big machines lined up in rows. A lot of those machines were based on inventions like the spinning jenny.
Who was James Watt?
James Watt improved the steam engine in the 1770s. His steam engine could power factories, pumps, and eventually trains, without needing to rely on water or wind.
What do you think changed for factory owners once they had steam power instead of water power?
They could build factories anywhere?
Exactly, they could build factories anywhere, not just next to rivers. That's a great point.
There's one more piece to this puzzle, and that's government and politics. Britain had a pretty stable government through the 1700s, with laws that protected private property and inventions.
What is a patent?
A patent is a legal document that protects an inventor's idea, so other people can't copy it and profit off it without permission.
What would happen if a country didn't have patent laws like this?
People might not want to invent things?
Good thinking, Derek. If inventors can't protect their ideas, they have less reason to spend time and money inventing, because anyone could just steal it.
Britain also had a strong banking system by this time, with banks willing to lend money to entrepreneurs who wanted to build factories and buy machines.
How might a strong banking system have helped industrialization move faster?
Business owners could borrow money for machines?
Exactly, Priya. Business owners could borrow the capital they needed instead of waiting years to save it up themselves.
Let's put all of this together. There were a lot of factors working at the same time in Britain, and that's part of why it happened there first.

We had population growth from the Agricultural Revolution, a large labor force from the enclosure movement, capital from trade and colonies, natural resources like coal and iron, new inventions like the spinning jenny and the steam engine, a stable government with patent laws, and a strong banking system.
What are the causes of the Industrial Revolution we talked about today?
Population growth.
Resources like coal and iron.
Capital and colonies.
Good job, all three of those are correct.
We also talked about new inventions, political stability, and banking, so there's a lot going on here, and that's kind of the point. No single cause explains the whole thing by itself.
How does one cause, like population growth, connect to another cause, like labor for factories?
More people meant more workers?
Exactly, more people meant more workers available for the new factories. Nice connection.
This is like when a bunch of different ingredients come together to make one dish. You need all of them, not just one, for it to really work.
So, back to our objective. By the end of class, you should be able to name at least three causes of industrialization and explain why Britain was first. I think we've covered that today.
Tomorrow we're going to look at how the Industrial Revolution changed daily life for workers, especially in factories and in cities.
Take out your notebooks and write down the three causes from today that stuck with you the most.
Okay, let's see what some of you wrote.
I wrote coal, iron, and inventions.
Nice work, Derek.
I wrote population, capital, and banking.
Good, Priya, those are solid choices.
Alright, go ahead and put your notebooks away. We'll pick this up again tomorrow.
Thanks for your focus today, I know eighth period is tough. I'll see you all next class.
Okay, eyes up here, everybody, let's get started.
Today we're going to look at factory working conditions during the Industrial Revolution, using a short piece of testimony from an actual factory worker.
By the end of today, you'll be able to make a claim about those conditions and back it up with evidence from the text.

Quick vocabulary word before we dive in — the factory system is defined as a method of production where workers and machines are brought together under one roof, usually owned by someone who isn't doing the labor himself.
In real life, think about a modern warehouse — same idea, just with way fewer protections back then.
So like an Amazon warehouse?
Kind of, yeah, but imagine none of the safety rules we have now.
Okay, here's what we're doing today. I'm handing out a half-sheet to each pair.
On it, you and your partner are going to write one claim about the working conditions, and one piece of evidence from the testimony that supports it.
First, thirty seconds on your own — just read the excerpt and write down one thing that stands out to you.
Alright, pens down for a second.
Now, work with your partner and agree on one claim and one piece of evidence from the testimony. You've got two and a half minutes.
Okay, let's bring it back together, eyes up here.
I'm not calling on individuals today, I want to hear from pairs. What did your pair put down?
We said the hours were really long, and the evidence was it said fourteen hours a day, six days a week.
Nice work. What evidence in the testimony backs that up?
It's the line where the worker says the bell rang before sunrise and she didn't get home till after dark.
I like how you pointed to the fourteen-hour day as evidence, not just said it was bad.
Great point. Who else — what did your pair put down?
We said children worked in the factories too, and the proof is it mentioned a boy named Thomas who was nine.
Good job. Why do you think children were hired?
Maybe because they were cheaper to pay than adults?
That's a strong guess — any other reasons?
Also their hands were smaller, so they could fix the machines when they got stuck.
Exactly, that's actually in a lot of the historical accounts. Well done.
Next pair — what did you two come up with?
Our claim was that the conditions were unsafe, and our evidence was the part about the machine that didn't have a guard on it.
How would a factory owner have answered that?
Probably he'd say putting guards on costs too much money?
Right, and that connects to something we'll keep seeing — profit versus safety.
Let's keep going. What did your pair put down?
We put that workers got punished for being late, and it said she lost a whole day's pay for being five minutes late once.
That's a great piece of evidence. I like how specific that number is.
What would happen if she tried to argue with the foreman about that?
She'd probably just get fired, honestly.
That's a fair point, and that's actually what happened to a lot of workers who spoke up.
Okay, next pair?
We weren't sure about ours.
